It's probably ignorance of a particular attack vector, but I'm not seeing what makes JSON schema validation *essential* as a primary control, especially given that it would expose you to god knows how much attack surface as a tradeoff.  It may be appropriate in some contexts to be explicit, but in large part, it is really duplicating the validation that would be done as recommended in section 5

* The typical JSON deserializer library that is secure will catch any JSON syntactical deviation so invalid JSON will not be accepted
* The typical JSON deserializer is already going to enforce most, if not all, of the structural validation of a JSON document based on the deserialization configuration directives or conventions of the JSON library. 
* 5.1.2 covers mass assignment risks already
* 5.1.4 covers validation of the individual data properties that would be inside the JSON payload
* Many cases in programming do not require deserialization to strongly-typed data; leaving values as maps and lists is sufficient and data can be validated as it is extracted and converted to the appropriate type, if necessary, or just leave as strings if that is all that is required.  Or using JSON parsing APIs to extract strings directly without marshaling to another data structure may be appropriate.

@jmanico can you help fill in the gaps that JSON schema validation addresses?

It's the additional attack surface tradeoff that I'm not sure I would say is always weighted toward adding this from a risk/reward standpoint.  If there is a compelling case where this kills whole classes of attacks that otherwise would be difficult to mitigate or left unmitigated, then by all means we should recommend it, but definitely not for L1 IMO.  I'm all for layered defenses, but would possibly see this as a nice-to-have defense-in-depth secondary control, not a primary control.

The fact that JSON schema is a moving target and who knows how complete the implementations are is a minor thing by comparison.
